title: Events and Messaging Architecture
readerIntent: Choose the correct local event, broker transport, persisted distribution, workflow, or scheduled execution contract.
priorKnowledge: Understand modules, services, runtime topology, and tenant context.
owner: nEvent listener runtime, nEms provider-neutral transport, NEMS persisted distribution, and each publishing/consuming module
summary: Nodics separates facts and listeners, cross-process transport, and durable distribution state so applications can evolve consumers without embedding vendor clients or a parallel event authority in business modules.

sections.heading: Architecture layers
items: Publisher: the authoritative module completes or atomically commits its business transition, then publishes a stable typed/versioned fact with tenant, source, trace, and approved context.
nEvent: loads and merges listener definitions and executes eligible in-process listeners. This is low overhead but not durable by itself.
nEms: exposes the provider-neutral messaging contract and selects the configured adapter. Publishers and listeners never import a broker client directly.
Provider adapter: maps connection, destination alias, serialization, publish/subscribe, acknowledgement, retry/error, readiness, reconnect, and close to a broker.
NEMS: owns persisted event definitions, distribution state, event logs, retry/failure state, and authorized manual recovery when durable distribution is selected.
Consumer: validates tenant, source, type/version, authorization, idempotency, and business state before calling its own services.

sections.heading: Choose the mechanism
items: Local listener when same-process best-effort reaction is sufficient and loss on crash is acceptable.
Broker transport when modules or infrastructure are separated and provider-qualified delivery is required.
Persisted NEMS distribution when the application needs durable state, retry evidence, event logs, replay/manual recovery, or cross-module outcome tracking.
Workflow when work is long-running, stateful, human-involved, approval-based, compensating, or requires visible business progress.
CronJob when execution is time-driven or needs scheduled reconciliation. These mechanisms may compose but must not duplicate one another's authority.

sections.heading: Event contract
items: Stable event type and version, owning publisher, allowed sources/targets, tenant/enterprise context, trace/correlation, occurrence time, schema, size limit, and safe headers.
Honest delivery guarantee such as best effort, at-most-once, or at-least-once; scope any ordering claim by destination/partition/key.
Consumer idempotency key, duplicate/redelivery behavior, compatibility policy, timeout, retry/backoff, poison-message isolation, failed/dead-letter state, replay authorization, and retention.
Payload minimization, classification, encryption, access, masking/redaction, residency, and deletion. Prefer governed references when full business data does not need to travel.

sections.heading: Lifecycle
items: Load governed listener and destination definitions from active modules and layered configuration.
Publish only after the authoritative transition succeeds; an event is evidence or a trigger, not an alternate persistence path.
Deliver locally and/or through the selected provider; persist NEMS state when configured.
Acknowledge success only after the consumer's owned acceptance boundary; otherwise record bounded retry or manual-recovery evidence.
On duplicate, crash, timeout, partition, or unknown outcome, reconcile the consumer's authoritative state before replay.
Drain stops new acquisition, allows bounded in-flight completion, and closes provider resources through the single lifecycle coordinator.

sections.heading: Security, operations, and proof
items: Use governed destination aliases and least-privilege service identities; do not accept request-supplied topics, queues, endpoints, credentials, or unrestricted targets.

Monitor publish/consume/success/failure/retry/replay/duplicate rates, end-to-end latency, backlog/oldest age, consumer lag, poison state, acknowledgements, throttling, reconnects, and provider health without logging protected payloads.

Test local versus transported behavior, serialization/version compatibility, authorization/tenant isolation, duplicate/idempotency, ordering, redelivery, poison handling, replay audit, backpressure, broker loss/reconnect, consumer crash, network partition, backlog recovery, drain, capacity, upgrade, and regression.
A provider scaffold or unit test is not production qualification; claimed guarantees require live evidence with the chosen broker and production-like topology.
